channels.name: nullbyte
channels.about: Programming deep-dives with the slides left in. Compilers, runtimes and the parts of the stack everyone skips.

channels.name: Analog Autopsy
channels.about: Repair benches, burnt capacitors and the occasional miracle. Vintage audio gear brought back to life.

channels.name: Wanderfoot
channels.about: Slow travel films. No narration, no music cues, just streets and the sound of them.

channels.name: Abyssal Field Notes
channels.about: Marine biology from the bottom up. Every film is cut from footage logged during research cruises.

channels.name: Crumb Culture
channels.about: Bread, mostly. Long ferments, simple flour and a very patient oven.

channels.name: lowlight audio
channels.about: Instrumentals for working, reading and staring out of windows. Original loops, free to stream.

channels.name: Pixel Archaeology
channels.about: Old games, old hardware, and the strange engineering decisions that made them work.

channels.name: Orbit Watch
channels.about: Launch coverage without the hype. Cameras we build, telemetry we decode, footage nobody else keeps.

channels.name: Stride Lab
channels.about: Endurance training logged honestly: the injuries, the spreadsheets and the long slow days.

videos.title: Writing a compiler from scratch — the whole walkthrough
videos.desc: A lexer, a parser and a stack machine, written in one sitting with the mistakes left in. We start from an empty file and end with something that can run a small language, then break it in all the interesting places.

captions.text: Okay, empty file. The only honest place to start a compiler video.
A lexer is a loop and a match statement. That is the entire trick.
Now we need a tree. Precedence climbing is twenty lines and a headache.

videos.title: Lexers are just state machines (live coding)
videos.desc: One state machine, eleven token types, and a lot of edge cases around strings and comments. Written from nothing, typed live, broken twice.
chapters: Strings, comments and the edge cases

captions.text: We are going to hand-roll this, because generated lexers hide the fun part.
Escape sequences. Everyone forgets escape sequences.

videos.title: The borrow checker, explained with a parking garage
videos.desc: One owner per value, many readers or one writer, and nothing outlives what it points at. We draw it as a parking garage and it stops being scary.

captions.text: Ownership is a parking policy. The garage does not care about your feelings.
You can have a hundred people reading the sign, or one person painting it.
A lifetime annotation is documentation, not a magic spell.

videos.title: Restoring a 1978 analog synth found in a barn
videos.desc: Forty years of dust, one dead power supply and a keyboard full of rust. Six weekends of work, condensed, ending with the first sound out of the speakers.
chapters: What came out of the barn

captions.text: This has been sitting in a barn since roughly 1989. Look at the keys.
The supply is a fire hazard, so that gets rebuilt before anything else.
Here goes. Volume up — if this hums, we have work to do.

videos.title: How a ladder filter actually shapes sound
videos.desc: Four poles, one feedback loop and the reason analog filters sound like they are alive. We sweep the same note through a scope so you can hear the difference.

captions.text: Every stage takes another 6 dB per octave off the top end.
The feedback path is where the character comes from.

videos.title: Kyoto at dusk — a quiet walking tour
videos.desc: Lanterns, wet stone and a pagoda on the skyline. Recorded on a single evening walk, no cuts, no narration — headphones recommended.

captions.text: Ambient audio only. The rain starts about halfway through.
That is a temple bell, not a train.

videos.title: The narrowest alley in Kyoto
videos.desc: Two buildings, one meter apart, and a whole street that lives in the gap. We walk it at closing time when the shops turn their lights off.

captions.text: You can touch both walls without trying.
The alley closes at nine. We are two minutes early.

videos.title: 4,000 meters down: what lives in the midnight zone
videos.desc: Below 1,000 meters there is no sunlight at all, and yet the water is full of animals. Footage from three research cruises, annotated with what the tags recorded.

captions.text: At this depth the sub is the only light source, and we keep it off.
This is not a plant. This is an animal the size of a bus.
The tag says it came up 300 meters overnight, every night.

videos.title: Bioluminescence is the ocean's private language
videos.desc: Almost everything down there can make light, and almost nothing can explain why two species bother. We look at the best guesses and the experiments behind them.

captions.text: Two chemicals and a protein. It is cheaper than swimming away.
Some of these flashes are bait, and some are a warning.

videos.title: 18 hours, four ingredients: the sourdough method
videos.desc: Flour, water, salt and time. The full method with the timings that actually matter, plus the two mistakes that turn a good loaf into a flat one.

captions.text: This starter is eight years old and has been left alone for a month.
Wet your hands, not the dough. It sticks less.
Twenty minutes lid on, twenty off. Listen for the crackle.

videos.title: Reviving a dead sourdough starter
videos.desc: A grey jar from the back of the fridge, a week of feeding, and the smell test that tells you whether it is worth saving.

captions.text: There is liquid on top and it smells like nail polish. Good start.
Twice a day, equal weights, warm spot. That is the whole protocol.

videos.title: lofi beats to debug to — single take
videos.desc: One loop, recorded in one pass at three in the morning. No drums, no vocals, nothing that asks for your attention.

captions.text: The rain is real. The piano is not a piano.
No need to watch. Just leave it running.

videos.title: Why CRT screens still feel better
videos.desc: Motion blur, phosphor decay and the fact that old games were drawn for a screen nobody owns anymore. We film a CRT at 960 frames per second to show what your eye actually saw.

captions.text: The blur is the feature. Developers relied on it.
At 960 frames per second you can watch the beam draw the image.

videos.title: Speedrunning a game I have never played
videos.desc: Twelve hours, one route document and a lot of deaths. The interesting part is not the record, it is how the community discovered the route in the first place.
chapters: The trick that skips a level

captions.text: The route doc is longer than the game.
One frame of input, and the level never loads.

videos.title: A dawn rocket launch, filmed at 1,000 fps
videos.desc: Our own cameras, twelve kilometers from the pad. Slowed down enough that you can see the shockwave leave the flame trench before the sound arrives.

captions.text: Three cameras, all armed by hand, none of them rated for this.
That white wall is condensation, not smoke. It is moving at the speed of sound.

videos.title: Why launches happen at dawn
videos.desc: It is not for the photographs. Orbital geometry, range scheduling and one very practical reason involving ice.

captions.text: The beautiful footage is a side effect, not a plan.
Vehicles that have been cold-soaked all night behave differently.

videos.title: My first 100 km: everything I got wrong
videos.desc: A full training block, unedited including the two months I was injured. Pacing errors, shoe changes, and the one session that actually mattered.

captions.text: This spreadsheet is from week three of eighteen.
Achilles, right side. I ignored it for eleven days.
Mile seventy is where the maths stops working.

videos.title: Running the coast road at sunrise
videos.desc: Twenty-two kilometers along a road that is only quiet before seven. Heart rate, pace and the morning fog, all logged.

captions.text: Zero people on this road. This is the whole reason I run here.
Nine hundred meters of climbing, spread across the last four k.
